passage: At volleyball practice in São Paulo, Coach Ramos watched Priscila set the ball and shook his head. "Left-handers can't be setters. Never works. Go back to the outside." He had coached for twenty years and said it like a fact. Priscila jogged back, cheeks burning. That night she couldn't stop thinking about it. Twenty years was a lot of years. But her friend Jana had shown her videos of a left-handed setter in the national league, and Priscila's own sets had landed well all week. The next day, stomach fluttering, she stayed after practice. "Coach, can I ask something? I found a left-handed setter in the national league. Could I try for two weeks?" Coach Ramos frowned for a long moment. "Two weeks," he said. "Then we see." She walked out feeling both stupid and brave.

qa.q: How long had Coach Ramos coached?
qa.a: He had coached for twenty years.

qa.q: Why did Priscila feel both stupid and brave walking out?
qa.a: Questioning a coach with twenty years' experience felt awkward and embarrassing, but she trusted the evidence enough to ask anyway.

qa.q: What made Priscila's question respectful?
qa.a: She asked privately after practice, brought a real example, and asked for a short trial instead of telling him he was wrong.

qa.q: How might Coach Ramos see Priscila's question?
qa.a: He might feel challenged at first, as his long frown shows, but respect her effort enough to give her two weeks.

grounding: A teenager weighs a sure-sounding coach's claim against evidence and, awkwardly, asks to test it.

passage: In the packed auditorium of the coaching centre, the director, introduced as "a gold medallist and national topper", told three hundred students, "If you sleep much at all, forget about the entrance exam." Pens scratched. Saurabh wrote it down too, then hesitated. Just last week the school's biology teacher had said teenagers need plenty of sleep to remember what they learn. Two sure voices, two different answers. After the talk, Saurabh caught Sonali by the water cooler. "Do you believe the no-sleep thing?" "He's a national topper," she said. "But is being a topper the same as knowing about sleep?" Saurabh asked, and immediately felt silly. Sonali paused. "Hm. Maybe ask Ma'am again?" He crossed out the note, then half rewrote it in pencil, just in case.

qa.q: How was the director introduced?
qa.a: As a gold medallist and national topper.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel silly after asking his question?
qa.a: Doubting a national topper in front of Sonali felt awkward, even though he suspected being a topper isn't the same as knowing about sleep.

qa.q: What is a good next step for Saurabh?
qa.a: He could go back to the biology teacher, whose view is the one to check with here, and look at where each claim comes from rather than trusting whoever sounds most impressive.

qa.q: Why might Sonali lean on the director's title at first?
qa.a: A confident speaker with a big title can feel safer to trust than her own doubt, though her pause shows she starts to question it too.

grounding: A teenager weighs a titled speaker's confident claim against a teacher's and awkwardly starts questioning whether titles guarantee truth.

passage:
Dear Sunaina di,
Something awkward happened. Papa forwarded a message to the whole family group saying every house must register on some website by Friday or the electricity will be cut. He sounded completely sure. He even called Chacha to make him do it. I've always thought Papa knows everything about this stuff; he handles all the bills.
But the website address looked strange, and it asked for bank details. I checked the electricity board's real site. Nothing about it, and there was even a warning about fake messages like this one.
I showed Papa at dinner. My voice was shaking. He went quiet, then said, "Hm, let me check," and later deleted the message from the group. He didn't say sorry, but he didn't scold me either.
Is it wrong that I feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
Nandini

qa.q: What did the website in the message ask for?
qa.a: It asked for bank details.

qa.q: Why does Nandini feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
qa.a: Nandini was right to check, which feels good, but correcting Papa, who handles all the bills, felt awkward and a little frightening.

qa.q: What made Nandini's approach sensible?
qa.a: Nandini checked the electricity board's real site, found the warning, and showed Papa calmly at dinner instead of arguing in the family group.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when shown the warning?
qa.a: Papa probably felt embarrassed after telling Chacha to register, which may be why he went quiet and deleted it without saying sorry.

grounding: A teenager checks a sure-sounding parent's forwarded message, finds it fake, and awkwardly corrects him.

passage:
Okay, Kiran, I'll tell you the whole embarrassing thing. I'm Baljeet, and I used to follow this study channel run by a guy who calls himself "Dr. Brain." White coat, fancy office, speaks like he's sure of everything. He said we only use ten percent of our brains, and his course "unlocks the rest."
I believed it. Why not? He's a doctor, right? So in biology class, when Mrs. Rao was talking about the brain, I put up my hand and said it. Like a fact. With confidence.
She smiled, not unkindly, and asked, "Where's that from?" Then she explained that scans show we use nearly all of it, just not all at once. The class laughed. My ears went red.
That evening I searched "Dr. Brain qualifications." Nothing. The white coat was just a coat. I unsubscribed, but I also felt weird, like, who else have I believed just because they sounded sure?

qa.q: What did 'Dr. Brain' say about how much of our brains we use?
qa.a: He said we only use ten percent of our brains.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet trust 'Dr. Brain' so easily?
qa.a: The white coat, fancy office and confident way of speaking, plus calling himself a doctor, made Baljeet feel he must know the truth.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do after the class laughed, and why was it a useful choice?
qa.a: Baljeet searched for 'Dr. Brain qualifications', found nothing, and unsubscribed, which is a way of checking a claim instead of trusting a title.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Rao have seen Baljeet's answer?
qa.a: Mrs. Rao seemed kind rather than mocking, asking where it came from, perhaps hoping Baljeet would learn to check sources.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting a confident online 'doctor', then awkwardly learning that titles and certainty do not guarantee truth.

passage:
I'm Santosh, Hansa's older brother, and I drive her to chess class on Saturdays. Her coach, Mr. Iyer, is a former state champion. Everyone treats his word like law. Last month he told her, "Always play this opening. It never loses."
Hansa, sixteen, played it in every game. Then she lost three in a row, all the same way. On the drive home she was quiet, then said, "Bhaiya, what if he's wrong?" and immediately, "No, he's a champion. It must be me."
That night I saw her at the dining table with the board, replaying the three games for hours.
Next Saturday, I waited outside the class. When she came out her cheeks were pink. "I showed him the line where it breaks," she said. "He went silent. Then he said, 'Hm. Show me again.'" She looked both proud and like she wanted to hide under the car seat.

qa.q: How many games in a row did Hansa lose with the opening?
qa.a: She lost three in a row, all the same way.

qa.q: What does Hansa saying 'No, he's a champion. It must be me' suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she trusted Mr. Iyer's title so much that she blamed herself first, and felt uneasy about doubting a champion.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that turned the doubt into something useful?
qa.a: She replayed the three games for hours to find where the opening breaks, then showed Mr. Iyer the exact line, giving evidence instead of just an opinion.

qa.q: How does Santosh see his sister after she comes out of class?
qa.a: Santosh sees her pink cheeks and senses she is both proud and embarrassed, which shows how awkward it felt to question someone she respects.

grounding: Told by a brother, it shows a teenager weighing whether to trust a confident champion coach and awkwardly learning a title doesn't guarantee being right.

passage: At the athletics club in Stockholm, Coach Anders was known for two things: winning medals and never being questioned. On the hottest day of the summer he told the group, "No water breaks today. Thirsty runners get tough." Nkechi, fifteen, felt her mouth go dry just hearing it. In biology last month they had learned that the body needs water when it sweats. But Anders had coached national runners. Who was she to argue? After the third lap her head started to pound. She stopped by the fence, face hot with embarrassment, and said, "Coach, I'm sorry, but my biology teacher said we need water in heat. Can I drink?" A few runners stared. Anders frowned, then waved a hand. "Fine. Everyone, two minutes." Nkechi drank, cheeks still burning, and her head began to clear.

qa.q: What did Coach Anders say about water?
qa.a: No water breaks today; thirsty runners get tough.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi's cheeks burn when she spoke up?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and nervous questioning a famous coach, even though she trusted what she had learned in biology.

qa.q: What made Nkechi's question respectful and effective?
qa.a: She apologised, gave her reason from biology and asked a simple question, so it didn't sound like an attack.

qa.q: How might the other runners feel after the water break?
qa.a: They were probably relieved and grateful, since they got water too because Nkechi spoke up.

grounding: A teenage girl weighs a famous coach's confident claim against what she learned in biology, and awkwardly questions it.

passage: The school auditorium was packed for the famous guest speaker, a young man with two million followers and a gold watch. "Toppers sleep four hours," he announced. "Sleep is for losers. I never slept in Class 12." Everyone cheered. Ojas wrote it down in capitals. That night he stayed up till 3 a.m. with physics, and the next day he fell asleep in the lab and spilled a beaker. Aditi ma'am, the biology teacher, sat with him at lunch. "Where did the four-hour idea come from?" "The speaker. He's really successful." "At what?" Ojas thought. "At... videos?" "Did he show any evidence about sleep?" Ojas felt his face go red. He had believed a gold watch. "No, ma'am." "Let's look at what the research says together," she said.

qa.q: What happened to Ojas in the lab the next day?
qa.a: He fell asleep and spilled a beaker.

qa.q: Why did Ojas's face go red at lunch?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, realising he had believed the speaker because of fame and a gold watch, with no evidence about sleep.

qa.q: What questions did Aditi ma'am ask, and why are they useful?
qa.a: Successful at what, and did he show evidence; they help Ojas separate someone's fame from whether a claim is true.

qa.q: How might Aditi ma'am feel about the speaker's message?
qa.a: She was probably concerned, since students like Ojas were copying an unhealthy idea.

grounding: A teenage boy believes a famous speaker's confident claim about sleep, then awkwardly learns that fame is not evidence.

passage:
Dear Kalyani didi,

passage: Pranav, you asked why I stopped listening to Coach on water breaks. So, you know I, Santosh, think Coach is a legend. State medals, loud whistle, everyone scared of him. And he told us, very sure, "No water during practice. Makes you tough." For two weeks I didn't drink. I felt dizzy on the long runs but I thought, he's the coach, he knows. Then last Thursday I almost fainted near the track. The school nurse gave me water and asked, "Beta, who told you not to drink?" I said Coach. She said being a coach doesn't make someone right about everything, and that she'd speak to him herself that day. She did. It was so awkward the next practice, Pranav. He didn't look at me. But then he blew the whistle for a water break.

passage:
Sunday. At lunch, Tanuja's father said, very sure, "Microwaves take the nutrition out of food. Everybody knows that." He was an engineer; he usually knew things. Tanuja nodded. Her friend Pranav, over for lunch, looked doubtful but kept eating.
Tuesday. In biology the teacher said heating in general can reduce some vitamins, and a microwave isn't worse than a stove, sometimes better, because it's quicker. Tanuja frowned. So Papa was wrong? But he'd sounded so sure. Maybe the teacher was wrong. She felt confused and oddly guilty for even thinking it.
Friday. At dinner Tanuja tried, awkwardly. "Papa, our teacher said microwaves aren't worse than the stove. How did you learn it?" He paused. "My colleague told me." "Could we look it up together?" He looked surprised, then laughed. "Fine. Bring the laptop."

qa.q: What did Tanuja's father say about microwaves on Sunday?
qa.a: Microwaves take the nutrition out of food. Everybody knows that.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling on Tuesday after the biology class?
qa.a: She felt confused and oddly guilty, torn between trusting Papa's sure voice and what the teacher said.

qa.q: How did Tanuja question her father well?
qa.a: She asked how he had learned it and suggested looking it up together, which respected him while checking the claim.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's father see her question on Friday?
qa.a: He seemed surprised at first, then amused and willing, since she asked politely rather than calling him wrong.

grounding: Shows a teenager awkwardly weighing whether to trust a confident parent, and learning that sounding sure is not the same as being right.

passage: Irfan, you're sixteen and you think every man on television with a suit and a loud voice must be right. Let your Vasudha Khala tell you about 1998. I was your age in Lucknow. A family friend, an engineer, very important, came to dinner. When I said I wanted to learn computers, he laughed. "Computers are a fad, beta. Do typing, or home science." He had a title, a car, a big voice. Everyone at the table agreed with him. I cried in the bathroom, then I nearly gave up. But my maths teacher asked me one question: "How does he know?" I didn't know. So I went to the library and read about the jobs coming. I took the computer course anyway, with my stomach in knots. Twenty-six years later I still run the IT office at the hospital. He was sure. He was wrong.

qa.q: What did the family friend tell young Vasudha to do instead of learning computers?
qa.a: Do typing, or home science.

qa.q: What was young Vasudha feeling after the dinner?
qa.a: She felt crushed and doubtful, crying in the bathroom and nearly giving up because an important man had laughed at her plan.

qa.q: Which moment in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Her maths teacher asking, "How does he know?", which sent her to the library to check the claim instead of trusting the title.

qa.q: How did everyone else at the dinner table respond to the engineer?
qa.a: They all agreed with him, trusting his title and loud voice without asking how he knew.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a teenager, nearly obeying an important man's confident claim, then checking it and learning that titles don't guarantee truth.

passage:
The district match was the next morning, and training ran late in the heat. Coach Farida blew her whistle. "No water breaks today. Real athletes train through thirst. It makes you tough."

Vikas's head was pounding. He knew from science class that the body needs water in heat. His cousin, a nurse, had said the same.

But Coach Farida had played for the state. Everyone said she knew everything. And she sounded so sure.

He looked at his bottle on the bench. If he drank, would he look weak? Would she drop him?

After fifteen more minutes he felt dizzy. He walked to the bench, drank, and said, awkwardly, "Sorry, Coach. My cousin's a nurse. She says we need water in the heat."

The team went silent. Farida frowned. Then, slowly, she said, "Everyone, water. Two minutes."

Vikas's face burned. But his head started to clear.

qa.q: What had Coach Farida played for?
qa.a: Coach Farida had played for the state.

qa.q: Why did Vikas hesitate to drink water?
qa.a: Vikas felt afraid of looking weak and being dropped, because the coach seemed so sure and had played for the state.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that was wise, even if awkward?
qa.a: Vikas drank water and politely mentioned his cousin's advice, looking after his health while respecting the coach.

qa.q: How might Coach Farida have felt when Vikas spoke up?
qa.a: Coach Farida may have felt surprised and a little challenged, but her call for a water break suggests she reconsidered.

grounding: The day before a match, a teenager weighs whether to trust a sure-sounding coach's unsafe rule, and awkwardly questions it.

passage:
Nilesh's mother, Tanuja, burst into his room. "Your exams are cancelled! It's in the family group. From the education minister himself."

Nilesh looked at the forwarded message. Bold letters, the state emblem, lots of exclamation marks.

His mother sounded so sure. She was a school principal. And the message looked official.

But something felt off. The date was wrong. There were spelling mistakes.

He hesitated. Correcting Ma felt awkward. She'd been right about so many things.

"Ma, can I just check the board website?"

"Why? It's from the minister."

He checked. No announcement. Then the board's official page had a note: "Fake message circulating. Exams as scheduled."

He showed her. She read it, went a little red, and laughed. "I believed it because it looked official."

"I almost believed it because you believed it," Nilesh said.

They both laughed, a bit awkwardly.

qa.q: What did the board's official page say?
qa.a: Fake message circulating. Exams as scheduled.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh hesitate before checking?
qa.a: Nilesh felt awkward and unsure, because his mother was a principal who sounded certain and correcting her felt disrespectful.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that was a good habit?
qa.a: Nilesh checked the official board website instead of trusting the message just because it looked official or his mother believed it.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on seeing the fake message notice?
qa.a: Tanuja felt a little embarrassed, going red, but then laughed about believing it.

grounding: A teenager weighs whether to trust his mother, a principal, about a forwarded message, and awkwardly checks the facts.

"Charu didi, look at this study influencer. She has two million followers."

"What's she saying, Anirban?"

"She says toppers never revise. Just read once and trust your brain. She topped her state."

"And you believe her?"

"She's a topper. She must know."

"She might be right for herself. But does she show any evidence it works for others?"

"...No. She just sounds really sure."

"Sounding sure isn't the same as being right. What does your teacher say?"

"Mrs Das says revise at least twice."

"And who has seen more students?"

"Mrs Das. Thirty years of students."

"So?"

Anirban scrolled down. The comments were full of people saying it didn't work for them. He hadn't noticed before.

"I feel stupid."

"Don't. Everyone falls for confident people. The trick is asking how they know."

qa.a: She has two million followers.

qa.q: Why was Anirban inclined to believe the influencer?
qa.a: Anirban felt impressed and trusting, because she was a topper who sounded very sure.

qa.q: What question did Charu didi suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Charu suggested asking how the influencer knows and whether there's evidence, which separates confidence from truth.

qa.q: How does Charu didi seem to see Anirban's mistake?
qa.a: Charu didi seems kind and understanding, telling him not to feel stupid because everyone falls for confident people.

grounding: A teenager weighs whether to trust a sure-sounding study influencer and learns, awkwardly, that titles don't guarantee truth.

passage: Last Christmas break, our school debate team trained every morning in the empty staff room, and Manoj sir ran everything. He had been a state champion once; we all practically worshipped him. On the third day he told me to open my speech with a "fact": that our country has the world's longest coastline. He said it so confidently that I wrote it down. That night I checked an atlas, and it said otherwise. I felt sick. Who was I to correct a state champion? The next morning I nearly stayed quiet. Then I said, very badly, "Sir, sorry, um, I think the atlas says... not us?" My face went hot. He frowned, checked, and laughed. "You're right, Himani. Good catch." I hadn't expected that. I've been checking things ever since, even when the person sounds very sure.

qa.q: What "fact" did Manoj sir tell Himani to open the speech with?
qa.a: That their country has the world's longest coastline.

qa.q: Why did Himani nearly stay quiet the next morning?
qa.a: Himani admired Manoj sir as a state champion and felt anxious and embarrassed about correcting him, as if a title made him automatically right.

qa.q: What helped Himani speak up, and what could make it easier next time?
qa.a: Having the atlas as evidence helped; next time Himani could show the source calmly and ask a question, keeping respect and truth together.

qa.q: How did Manoj sir react to being corrected?
qa.a: He frowned, checked, then laughed and said "Good catch," showing he cared more about accuracy than about always being right.

grounding: Shows a teenager weighing whether to trust a confident coach, and awkwardly learning that a title does not guarantee a fact is true.
